## Prerequisite and foundational solutions

### Julia essentials for modelers

#### Solution to Exercise 1 {#solution-p01-ex1}

We extend the in-place kernel with a fourth state $C$ whose derivative is the
force of infection times $S$, i.e. the instantaneous incidence $\lambda S$. Since
new infections *leave* $S$ at exactly the rate they *enter* $C$, we expect
`du[4] == -du[1]`.

```{julia}
#| label: sol-p01-ex1
function sir_incidence!(du, u, p, t)
    S, I, R, C = u
    λ = p.β * p.c * I / p.N
    du[1] = -λ * S
    du[2] = λ * S - p.γ * I
    du[3] = p.γ * I
    du[4] = λ * S            # cumulative incidence
    return nothing
end

u0 = [990.0, 10.0, 0.0, 0.0]
p  = (β = 0.05, c = 10.0, γ = 0.25, N = 1000.0)
du = zeros(4)
sir_incidence!(du, u0, p, 0.0)
(du = du, matches = isapprox(du[4], -du[1]; atol = 1e-12))
```

The check returns `true`: cumulative incidence grows at precisely the rate the
susceptible pool depletes, because both equal $\lambda S$. The recovered term
$\gamma I$ does not enter $C$ — recovery is a separate flow out of $I$.

#### Solution to Exercise 2 {#solution-p01-ex2}

`rand` returns uniform draws on $[0,1)$, so the fraction below a threshold $q$
estimates $q$ itself. Here $q = 1 - e^{-0.25}\approx 0.221$.

```{julia}
#| label: sol-p01-ex2
using StableRNGs
rate_to_proportion(r, δt) = -expm1(-r * δt)

rng = StableRNG(2024)
draws = rand(rng, 10_000)
q = rate_to_proportion(0.25, 1.0)
fraction = count(<(q), draws) / length(draws)   # broadcasting via count(<(q), ·)
(target = q, observed = fraction, absolute_error = abs(fraction - q))
```

The observed fraction sits within about $0.01$ of the target. Because the stream
is produced by a *local* `StableRNG(2024)`, whose algorithm is fixed across Julia
versions and platforms, every reader obtains the identical `draws` vector and the
identical fraction — the figure is bit-for-bit reproducible, unlike one seeded
through the global `default_rng()`.

### Probability and stochastic processes

#### Solution to Exercise 1 {#solution-p02-ex1}

The Binomial$(n,p)$ variance is $np(1-p)$. We compare the sample variance of
100 000 draws against this value for two probabilities.

```{julia}
#| label: sol-p02-ex1
using Distributions, StableRNGs, Statistics

function variance_check(n, p; seed = 7, nsamples = 100_000)
    rng = StableRNG(seed)
    samples = [rand(rng, Binomial(n, p)) for _ in 1:nsamples]
    (theoretical = n * p * (1 - p), empirical = var(samples))
end

low  = variance_check(990, 0.02)
half = variance_check(990, 0.50)
(p_002 = low, p_050 = half)
```

Both empirical variances match $np(1-p)$ closely. Viewed as a function of $p$,
$np(1-p)$ is a downward parabola maximised at $p = 0.5$: the outcome of each
Bernoulli trial is then maximally uncertain (a fair coin), so the sum fluctuates
most. Near $p = 0$ or $p = 1$ almost every trial has the same outcome and the
variance collapses — hence the $p = 0.5$ case has by far the larger spread.

#### Solution to Exercise 2 {#solution-p02-ex2}

We rerun the ensemble at the coarse ($\delta t = 1$) and fine ($\delta t = 0.1$)
steps over the same 40-day horizon and record the extinction fraction.

```{julia}
#| label: sol-p02-ex2
using Distributions, StableRNGs
rate_to_proportion(r, δt) = -expm1(-r * δt)

function chain_step(state, p, δt, rng)
    S, I, R = state; β, c, γ, N = p
    Y = rand(rng, Binomial(S, rate_to_proportion(β * c * I / N, δt)))
    Z = rand(rng, Binomial(I, rate_to_proportion(γ, δt)))
    (S - Y, I + Y - Z, R + Z)
end

function extinction_fraction(δt; nsims = 200, horizon = 40.0)
    p = (0.05, 10.0, 0.25, 1000); nsteps = round(Int, horizon / δt)
    extinct = 0
    for seed in 1:nsims
        rng = StableRNG(seed); s = (990, 10, 0)
        faded = false
        for _ in 1:nsteps
            s = chain_step(s, p, δt, rng)
            s[2] == 0 && (faded = true)
        end
        faded && (extinct += 1)
    end
    extinct / nsims
end

(coarse_dt1 = extinction_fraction(1.0), fine_dt0_1 = extinction_fraction(0.1))
```

Extinction is rare at $R_0 = 2$: no realisation faded out at $\delta t = 1$,
while a small fraction did at $\delta t = 0.1$. Finer steps change the discrete
dynamics because the per-step probabilities $p_I, p_R$ are *nonlinear* in
$\delta t$: a single coarse step lumps together events that finer steps resolve
individually, and the binomial construction cannot let an individual become
infected *and* recover within one step. Resolving the early phase in smaller
increments exposes more chances for the last infective to recover before
transmitting, so the finer grid detects the occasional fade-out the coarse grid
misses. As $\delta t \to 0$ these artefacts vanish and the chain approaches the
exact continuous-time Markov process.

### Calculus and numerical methods

#### Solution to Exercise 1 {#solution-p03-ex1}

The midpoint (RK2) method evaluates the derivative at a half-step to cancel the
leading error term, giving second-order global accuracy.

```{julia}
#| label: sol-p03-ex1
function sir_ode!(du, u, p, t)
    S, I, R = u; β, c, γ, N = p
    λ = β * c * I / N
    du[1] = -λ * S; du[2] = λ * S - γ * I; du[3] = γ * I; return nothing
end

function midpoint(f, u0, p, δt, tmax)
    ts = 0.0:δt:tmax
    us = Matrix{Float64}(undef, length(u0), length(ts)); us[:, 1] .= u0
    k1 = similar(u0); k2 = similar(u0)
    for n in 1:length(ts) - 1
        u = @view us[:, n]
        f(k1, u, p, ts[n])
        f(k2, u .+ (δt / 2) .* k1, p, ts[n] + δt / 2)
        us[:, n + 1] .= u .+ δt .* k2
    end
    collect(ts), us
end

u0 = [990.0, 10.0, 0.0]; p = (0.05, 10.0, 0.25, 1000.0); tmax = 40.0
_, ref = midpoint(sir_ode!, u0, p, tmax / 2^13, tmax); u_ref = ref[:, end]
δts = [tmax / 2^k for k in 5:10]
errs = map(δt -> maximum(abs.(midpoint(sir_ode!, u0, p, δt, tmax)[2][:, end] .- u_ref)), δts)
orders = [log2(errs[k] / errs[k + 1]) for k in 1:length(errs) - 1]
(mean_order = sum(orders) / length(orders), close_to_2 = isapprox(sum(orders) / length(orders), 2.0; atol = 0.2))
```

The mean empirical order is close to 2 — one higher than forward Euler — so
halving the step now cuts the error roughly fourfold rather than twofold.

#### Solution to Exercise 2 {#solution-p03-ex2}

First the relative error in $I$ at $\delta t = 0.1$, using a fine Euler reference;
then a search for the largest step keeping every compartment nonnegative.

```{julia}
#| label: sol-p03-ex2
function euler(f, u0, p, δt, tmax)
    ts = 0.0:δt:tmax
    us = Matrix{Float64}(undef, length(u0), length(ts)); us[:, 1] .= u0
    du = similar(u0)
    for n in 1:length(ts) - 1
        f(du, @view(us[:, n]), p, ts[n]); us[:, n + 1] .= us[:, n] .+ δt .* du
    end
    collect(ts), us
end

_, ref2 = euler(sir_ode!, u0, p, tmax / 2^13, tmax); Iref = ref2[2, end]
_, u01 = euler(sir_ode!, u0, p, 0.1, tmax)
rel_err_I = abs(u01[2, end] - Iref) / Iref

nonneg(δt) = all(≥(0), euler(sir_ode!, u0, p, δt, tmax)[2])
candidates = 0.1:0.2:6.0
largest_stable = maximum(δt for δt in candidates if nonneg(δt))
(relative_error_I = rel_err_I, largest_nonnegative_step = largest_stable)
```

The relative error in the infectious compartment at $\delta t = 0.1$ is a fraction
of a percent. Beyond a critical step size, forward Euler overshoots and drives a
compartment negative — an instability the reported `largest_nonnegative_step`
locates. This conditional stability, not accuracy alone, is why adaptive solvers
are preferred.

### Foundations: SIR theory and the Julia workflow

#### Solution to Exercise 1 {#solution-ch01-ex1}

Holding $\beta = 0.05$ and $\gamma = 0.25$, $R_0 = \beta c/\gamma$ scales linearly
with the contact rate. The threshold $R_0 = 1$ occurs at $c = \gamma/\beta = 5$.

```{julia}
#| label: sol-ch01-ex1
using NonlinearSolve, DataFrames

β, γ, N = 0.05, 0.25, 1000.0     # c is the swept quantity, so no parameter tuple here
s₀ = 990.0 / N
attack(R0) = 1 - solve(NonlinearProblem((s, r) -> s - s₀ * exp(-r * (1 - s)), 0.2, R0), NewtonRaphson()).u

DataFrame(c = [4, 6, 8, 10],
          R0 = [β * c / γ for c in (4, 6, 8, 10)],
          attack_rate = [round(attack(β * c / γ); digits = 3) for c in (4, 6, 8, 10)])
```

For $c = 4$ we have $R_0 = 0.8 < 1$ and the attack rate ($\approx 0.045$) barely
exceeds the initial 1% seed — the few initial infections cannot sustain a chain
of transmission, so no epidemic occurs. For $c \ge 6$ ($R_0 \ge 1.2$) a genuine
epidemic develops and the attack rate climbs steeply with $R_0$. The switch
happens exactly at $c = 5$, where $R_0 = 1$: below it each infection produces
fewer than one secondary case on average.

#### Solution to Exercise 2 {#solution-ch01-ex2}

We locate the infectious peak and read off the susceptible fraction there; theory
predicts $S/N = 1/R_0$.

```{julia}
#| label: sol-ch01-ex2
using OrdinaryDiffEq
function sir_ode!(du, u, p, t)
    S, I, R = u; λ = p.β * p.c * I / p.N
    du[1] = -λ * S; du[2] = λ * S - p.γ * I; du[3] = p.γ * I; return nothing
end

u0 = [990.0, 10.0, 0.0]
p  = (β = 0.05, c = 10.0, γ = 0.25, N = 1000.0)
sol = solve(ODEProblem(sir_ode!, u0, (0.0, 80.0), p), Tsit5(); saveat = 0.1)
I = sol[2, :]; R0 = p.β * p.c / p.γ
peak_ok = isapprox(sol[1, argmax(I)] / p.N, 1 / R0; atol = 0.01)

p_crit = merge(p, (γ = 0.5,))        # R0 = 1
sol_crit = solve(ODEProblem(sir_ode!, u0, (0.0, 80.0), p_crit), Tsit5(); saveat = 0.1)
(R0 = R0, S_over_N_at_peak = sol[1, argmax(I)] / p.N, threshold_ok = peak_ok,
 peak_I_baseline = round(maximum(I); digits = 1),
 peak_I_R0eq1 = round(maximum(sol_crit[2, :]); digits = 1))
```

At the baseline $R_0 = 2$ the susceptible fraction at the peak equals $1/R_0 = 0.5$
to within 1%, confirming @eq-ch01-threshold. Raising $\gamma$ to $0.5$ makes
$R_0 = 1$: the growth rate $\lambda S - \gamma I$ is negative from the outset
because $S/N = 0.99 < 1 = 1/R_0$ only marginally, and prevalence merely decays
from its initial value — there is no epidemic wave, only monotone extinction of
the initial infectives.

### Discrete-time models

#### Solution to Exercise 1 {#solution-ch02-ex1}

We compare the deterministic map and the stochastic-chain mean against a
high-accuracy ODE reference at $\delta t = 1$ and $\delta t = 0.25$.

```{julia}
#| label: sol-ch02-ex1
using Distributions, StableRNGs, OrdinaryDiffEq
rate_to_proportion(r, δt) = -expm1(-r * δt)
function map_step(s, p, δt)
    S, I, R = s
    inf = rate_to_proportion(p.β * p.c * I / p.N, δt) * S
    rec = rate_to_proportion(p.γ, δt) * I
    (S - inf, I + inf - rec, R + rec)
end
function chain_step(s, p, δt, rng)
    S, I, R = s
    Y = rand(rng, Binomial(round(Int, S), rate_to_proportion(p.β * p.c * I / p.N, δt)))
    Z = rand(rng, Binomial(round(Int, I), rate_to_proportion(p.γ, δt)))
    (S - Y, I + Y - Z, R + Z)
end
function run_traj(step, u0, p, δt, n; extra = ())
    traj = Matrix{Float64}(undef, 3, n + 1); traj[:, 1] .= u0; s = Tuple(float.(u0))
    for k in 1:n; s = step(s, p, δt, extra...); traj[:, k + 1] .= s; end
    traj
end

function sir_ode!(du, u, p, t)
    S, I, R = u; λ = p.β * p.c * I / p.N
    du[1] = -λ * S; du[2] = λ * S - p.γ * I; du[3] = p.γ * I; return nothing
end
p = (β = 0.05, c = 10.0, γ = 0.25, N = 1000.0)
ode_peak = maximum(solve(ODEProblem(sir_ode!, [990.0, 10, 0], (0.0, 40.0), p), Tsit5(); saveat = 0.05)[2, :])

function peaks(δt; nsims = 60)
    n = round(Int, 40 / δt)
    map_peak = maximum(run_traj((s, p, d) -> map_step(s, p, d), [990, 10, 0], p, δt, n)[2, :])
    ens = [run_traj(chain_step, [990, 10, 0], p, δt, n; extra = (StableRNG(s),)) for s in 1:nsims]
    chain_mean_peak = maximum(vec(sum(reduce(hcat, (t[2, :] for t in ens)); dims = 2)) ./ nsims)
    (map_peak = round(map_peak; digits = 1), chain_mean_peak = round(chain_mean_peak; digits = 1))
end

(ode_peak = round(ode_peak; digits = 1), dt1 = peaks(1.0), dt025 = peaks(0.25))
```

The deterministic map at $\delta t = 0.25$ lands much closer to the ODE peak
($\approx 158$) than at $\delta t = 1$, because the map is a first-order
(forward-Euler-like) discretisation whose error shrinks with the step. The
stochastic-chain mean lies close to the map at each step size — it is the map's
random counterpart — but its peak is additionally *lowered* by peak-timing
jitter: individual epidemics crest at slightly different times, so averaging them
flattens the ensemble-mean peak, which can therefore sit even nearer to (or just
below) the ODE value than the map does. Either way, refining $\delta t$ moves both
discrete peaks toward the continuous-time reference.

#### Solution to Exercise 2 {#solution-ch02-ex2}

Extinction probability is the fraction of realisations reaching $I = 0$ before day
40, computed at two contact rates.

```{julia}
#| label: sol-ch02-ex2
function extinction(c; nsims = 200, δt = 1.0)
    p = (β = 0.05, c = c, γ = 0.25, N = 1000.0); n = round(Int, 40 / δt); extinct = 0
    for seed in 1:nsims
        rng = StableRNG(seed); s = (990, 10, 0); faded = false
        for _ in 1:n; s = chain_step(s, p, δt, rng); s[2] == 0 && (faded = true); end
        faded && (extinct += 1)
    end
    extinct / nsims
end
(R0_2_c10 = extinction(10.0), R0_1_2_c6 = extinction(6.0),
 R0 = (0.05 * 10 / 0.25, 0.05 * 6 / 0.25))
```

Lowering the contact rate from $c = 10$ ($R_0 = 2$) to $c = 6$ ($R_0 = 1.2$)
raises the extinction probability sharply. With a smaller $R_0$ each infectious
individual produces fewer secondary cases, so the early stochastic phase — when
only a handful are infected — is far more likely to fizzle out before an epidemic
establishes. This fade-out is a purely stochastic phenomenon: the deterministic
map, lacking integer counts, always predicts a (small) deterministic outbreak and
can never reach exactly zero.

### Ordinary differential equations

#### Solution to Exercise 1 {#solution-ch03-ex1}

We sweep the lockdown strength, using a `ContinuousCallback` on $\mathrm{d}I/
\mathrm{d}t$ to detect turning points, and report the epidemic peak (largest $I$
among detected events).

```{julia}
#| label: sol-ch03-ex1
using OrdinaryDiffEq, DiffEqCallbacks, DataFrames
function sir_ode!(du, u, p, t)
    S, I, R = u; λ = p.β * p.c * I / p.N
    du[1] = -λ * S; du[2] = λ * S - p.γ * I; du[3] = p.γ * I; return nothing
end
u0 = [990.0, 10.0, 0.0]; tspan = (0.0, 80.0); t1, t2 = 10.0, 30.0
p = (β = 0.05, c = 10.0, γ = 0.25, N = 1000.0)
dIdt(u, p) = (p.β * p.c * u[2] / p.N) * u[1] - p.γ * u[2]

function peak_under(β_lock)
    events = Tuple{Float64,Float64}[]
    set_β!(i, β) = (i.p = merge(i.p, (β = β,)))
    peak_cb = ContinuousCallback((u, t, i) -> dIdt(u, i.p), i -> push!(events, (i.t, i.u[2])))
    set = CallbackSet(PresetTimeCallback([t1], i -> set_β!(i, β_lock)),
                      PresetTimeCallback([t2], i -> set_β!(i, 0.05)),
                      peak_cb)
    solve(ODEProblem(sir_ode!, u0, tspan, p), Tsit5();
          callback = set, reltol = 1e-8, abstol = 1e-8)
    t_peak, I_peak = argmax(e -> e[2], events)
    (t_peak = round(t_peak; digits = 2), I_peak = round(I_peak; digits = 1))
end

DataFrame(β_lock = [0.045, 0.035, 0.025, 0.015],
          peak_time = [peak_under(b).t_peak for b in (0.045, 0.035, 0.025, 0.015)],
          peak_I = [peak_under(b).I_peak for b in (0.045, 0.035, 0.025, 0.015)])
```

Stronger lockdowns (smaller $\beta_\text{lock}$) do not simply lower the peak: the
detected peak height and timing behave *non-monotonically*. Moderate lockdowns
(e.g. $\beta_\text{lock}=0.035$) suppress transmission during the window, cutting
the peak while it still occurs near the intervention. But very strong lockdowns
defer the epidemic almost entirely: with growth stifled between days 10 and 30,
susceptibles are "saved" and the wave resurges *after* the lockdown lifts —
pushing the peak time out to ~50–60 days and, because a larger susceptible pool
is preserved, allowing the rebound peak to climb again for the most aggressive
setting. This is the flatten-*and-delay* trade-off with a sting in the tail: a
temporary intervention reshapes and postpones the epidemic rather than removing
it, and the strongest short lockdown is not necessarily the one with the lowest
overall peak.

#### Solution to Exercise 2 {#solution-ch03-ex2}

We augment the system with cumulative incidence $C$ and reconstruct daily
incidence from the dense interpolant.

```{julia}
#| label: sol-ch03-ex2
function sir_cumulative!(du, u, p, t)
    S, I, R, C = u; λ = p.β * p.c * I / p.N
    du[1] = -λ * S; du[2] = λ * S - p.γ * I; du[3] = p.γ * I; du[4] = λ * S; return nothing
end
p = (β = 0.05, c = 10.0, γ = 0.25, N = 1000.0)
sol = solve(ODEProblem(sir_cumulative!, [990.0, 10.0, 0.0, 0.0], (0.0, 80.0), p),
            Tsit5(); reltol = 1e-9, abstol = 1e-9)

days = 1:80
daily = [sol(t)[4] - sol(t - 1)[4] for t in days]     # C(t) − C(t−1)
(final_C = round(sol(80.0)[4]; digits = 3),
 sum_daily = round(sum(daily); digits = 3),
 reconstructs = isapprox(sum(daily), sol(80.0)[4] - sol(0.0)[4]; atol = 1e-6))
```

The daily increments are differences of the cumulative-incidence interpolant, and
their sum telescopes to $C(80) - C(0)$. The check confirms the reconstruction to
machine tolerance, illustrating that the dense output `sol(t)` can be resampled
onto any grid — here the integer-day grid used to compare a continuous model with
daily surveillance data, a pattern the observation-model chapter builds on.
